chapters.title: Five questions — a survey of our reactions

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: So we're going to do some exercises now. This could be a ten-week workshop. Maybe we'll do a V Houses workshop and charge a lot of money for it. But the idea here is to just maybe start identifying: what do we think is holding us back? So maybe get a phone out, or something to write on, just to take notes. Don't look at your Instagram, please — that's another form of affliction.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: And these questions actually came from a conversation I had with a good friend of mine. We were talking about how we respond to other people's successes. So I'm going to ask a question, and I want you to answer honestly — try to think about when this happened in your life.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: Here's the question.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: (1) When I see somebody confidently living with other people or engaging with other people, I think they must be ______. When I see someone comfortable with other people, I think they must be ______. What do you think about those people? Just write it down.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: All right, next question.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: (2) When I come across someone who has a lot more money than I do, I assume ______. It can be about them or yourself.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: Next question — wait, wait, she has lots of things to say. All right.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: (3) When I see someone who's in a happy romantic relationship, I think that couple probably ______. Be really honest. Don't be a Dharma practitioner — "I'm such a good person."

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: Okay, we'll do one more.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: (4) When I see someone getting more attention than me — like my teacher paying attention to another student, I assume ______. What do I think?

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: All right, last one. (5) When someone gives me advice that I actually need, my reaction to that advice is ______.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: All right, so we're going to take a little survey. We did one, two, three, four, five questions. Were all of your answers positive? Okay — thank God. If they were all positive, I'd say you can go somewhere else. Were any of them positive? Okay. Did anyone have all negatives? Okay, cool. This is working. This is exactly what I hoped would happen.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: So now take inventory. The things you thought were positive — that's probably an area you don't really have to work on too much. But for the things you had a negative reaction about, now you've got to be like, why?

chapters.title: It's more about you than them

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: And this came out of a conversation I had with a friend. They were feeling really upset at themselves, because when they see someone in a really good relationship, they always have these other kinds of thoughts. Like, "well, they're happy, but they don't know about seeds." {audience laughs} You laugh — there he is. But watch how your Dharma practice turns into an affliction. Because now you're better than them?

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: Like, when someone gives me advice that I need — there are many different kinds of reactions. For me, it depends on who's giving me the advice. Are there people in your life who give you advice and you're just like, bring it on, I love it, tell me more? And then when your mom tells you something — right? How strong of a reaction do you have when mom tells you you're not doing the dishes right? You're carrying that with you all the time. That is in you. If someone can piss you off in 0.01 seconds…

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: Why is it that with my Lama — the other day we were having a meeting, and I was talking to someone else about the transmission, and he's sitting next to me. He was doing something else. And I had this — you start developing a sixth sense about your teacher. I was like, he's going to start talking. And as I felt that, I was like, oh, he's starting to talk. And I sat back. I turned my body. And I just went quiet. We'll talk about the relationship with the teacher another time. And he said to me — well, I said, oh, I'm sorry, I was talking over you. And he said, no, no, I interrupted you. But I'm like — sorry, that was my fault. Totally relaxed, chill. I can be with that person all the time, no problem.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: But there are people who, immediately when they interrupt me — even if it's relevant — I'm like a Tyrannosaurus rex. Why? Why, with one person, can I be so like, oh, you can interrupt me whenever you want, and with another all these feelings come up around the interruption? The faster you get angry…

chapters.title: The Juan story — anger and patience

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: The other day, I got really mad at Juan. And I went from zero to — and I was watching myself do it. I'm like, why are you doing this to me? Because when he finished his original sentence, I wouldn't have gotten upset. But why did that come out like that? I apologized right afterwards, and I think he forgives me — I don't know how he really feels about it, but I felt terrible. I went back and I'm like, why? Why didn't I have patience at all? What was I defending? What was I protecting? What was not safe? What couldn't I control? All of those questions came up, and I went into a big, deep exploration. So, thank you, Juan.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: He actually did nothing wrong. He was actually trying to help somebody. But I saw it as — right? — before I waited until I got more information and got curious about why he was saying what he was saying. One word can destroy a friendship, a relationship of many, many years. I want to be friends with Juan. I love Juan. Even when we say, where's Juan? — the fact that we ask that question means we want him around. We can't find him — but that's Juan Jasso. You never really know where Juan is. But we want him around. And I want that friendship with him. And if I did that anger at him all the time, I could lose that friendship. But that's what we do all the time, because those emotions just take over.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: So those five questions — there are more kinds of questions like that. And then we've got to investigate: well, why? Like, when I see someone who has a lot more money than I do, what do I assume? They worked harder. Maybe they were unethical. Maybe they're trust-fund babies. I'm creating a story about them that's actually more about me than about them.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: Don't make that joke, Tim. I want to get back home. I want to be led through immigration.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: So let's investigate. We're going to investigate five categories of things where you might find limiting beliefs about yourself — what's operating, what's in your operating system? Some of it might resonate with you, some of it may not. Remember when I said some of those responses were positive and some were negative? The negative ones are informing you that that's something holding you back.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: Like, if you see a couple in a good relationship and you're just like, can I join? — just kidding — great, congratulations, I'm so happy for you, then that's probably not your issue. But if you're looking at couples and you're like, they're not really happy, all couples have problems, they're just faking happiness, when they go home he's going to get yelled at by his wife — but if you start thinking, well, they can't possibly be that way, the reality is not what it looks like — God, what kind of negative seeds are you really planting? You are tartuking about the wrong thing. You're planting those seeds over and over again, and you don't even see it. So many of these things are so automatic that you're tartuking about it all the time, and your operating system is never upgrading.

chapters.title: Noticing is what starts the change

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: So we have to first become aware of the things we're tartuking about that are keeping our operating system in Microsoft DOS — some old software. "Things happen because I'm too old." You're not that old. Yeah, well, you didn't know that software reference. You can't upgrade your operating system.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: So the idea is to look at these things and bring awareness to them. And then if you have the habit of being like, oh, they're not really happy, and you notice yourself doing it — the noticing is the first thing that starts the change. Because then you get to start investigating: well, why do I think that? Why do I think that all relationships are unhappy? Because that's what it says — "they must be unhappy." And so you're constantly looking for unhappiness. And you're going to find reasons why your own relationship will not be happy. And then the real work happens.
